summary: Describes a baseline BATched Sparse coding scheme for multi-hop networks. It combines a fountain-code-like outer code with batch-based linear network coding, and discusses research issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets are mixed together a bit at each stop so that losses along a long route are easier to recover from.

questions: how does network coding improve wireless delivery
fountain codes and linear network coding
subtitle: Linear network coding that mixes packets to recover from losses across multiple hops

tldr.problem: Multi-hop wireless networks lose packets along the route; traditional transport protocols that rely on end-to-end retransmission or hop-by-hop error correction alone struggle with unreliable links and accumulating losses.
tldr.mechanism: BATS (BATched Sparse) coding combines a fountain-code-like outer code with linear network coding as an inner code, allowing intermediate nodes to mix received packets before forwarding them, so lost packets can be recovered without waiting for retransmission.
tldr.outcome: Data delivery improves in multi-hop networks without requiring highly reliable point-to-point links, making BATS suitable for wireless mesh networks, underwater acoustic networks, and sensor networks.

today: RFC 9426 is an Informational document from the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), published in July 2023. It represents the baseline BATS coding scheme and research directions; it is not a standards-track specification and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: How BATS Improves Delivery in Unreliable Networks
sections.content:
BATched Sparse (BATS) coding is a linear network coding scheme combining two layers: an outer code (a matrix generalization of fountain codes like RaptorQ) and an inner code (hop-by-hop linear network coding called recoding).

Traditional approaches have drawbacks. End-to-end retransmission (like TCP) suffers in multi-hop networks because each lost packet requires waiting for an entire round-trip time to the destination and back. Hop-by-hop forward error correction (FEC) adds overhead at each hop independently, and network hops may not retransmit if data is not needed there.

BATS combines the benefits of both: the source encodes data once using the outer code (end-to-end), but intermediate nodes also perform linear combinations of packets on the same batch (hop-by-hop recoding). This means intermediate nodes can create new coded packets from packets they receive, mixing loss recovery information forward without waiting for retransmission requests. The destination decodes using both layers jointly.

BATS is suitable for wireless mesh and ad hoc networks (vehicular, sensor, smart infrastructure), underwater acoustic networks (where long propagation delays make feedback inefficient and point-to-point links are extremely unreliable), and content distribution systems using network coding.
sections.plainLanguage: At each stop on a long path, mix up the packets you got with math before sending them on. That way, even if some packets get lost on the next hop, the destination can unmix them. No need to wait for "resend that."

sections.title: BATS Data Model and Encoding
sections.content:
BATS processes data in batches. The source node first partitions data into K source packets of T octets each, padding the last packet. The outer encoder then generates M coded packets per batch, each derived from a random subset of source packets using matrix operations in finite fields. Each coded packet includes a coefficient vector (metadata indicating which source packets are mixed in) and the coded data.

A key concept is degree: the number of source packets combined to create a batch. The encoder samples a degree from a degree distribution and randomly selects that many source packets. For example, a degree of 3 means three source packets are mixed together using coefficients from Galois field GF(256).

Each batch has an ID (BID) that stays with packets as they traverse the network. Batches are processed independently, so intermediate nodes can mix packets within the same batch but do not mix across different batches.

Recommended parameters balance performance and computation cost. When q=2 (binary field), batch sizes M should be 16, 32, 64, or 128. When q=256 (larger field), M should be 4, 8, 16, or 32. The number of source packets K should be at least 128.
sections.plainLanguage: Break data into chunks. Mix a few chunks together using math, creating coded packets. Each coded packet remembers which chunks went into it. Send batches of coded packets down the path.

sections.title: Hop-by-Hop Recoding and Decoding
sections.content:
At each intermediate node, recoding mixes received coded packets to create new coded packets. Unlike the source encoder (which mixes source packets), a recoder mixes already-coded packets using random coefficients in the finite field.

Systematic recoding is a practical variant: instead of recombining all received packets randomly, the recoder forwards the packets it received directly (these are systematic, or unchanged packets) and generates only a few new combinations. This reduces computation cost and latency compared to fully random recoding, making it suitable for multi-hop scenarios.

At the destination, the outer decoder uses a belief propagation algorithm to recover the K source packets. It processes batches one at a time: when it finds a batch it can decode (where the coefficient matrix has full rank), it solves the linear equations to recover the source packets that went into it. It then substitutes these known packets into remaining, partially-decodable batches, reducing their degrees and eventually allowing more batches to decode. This process continues until all source packets are recovered or no more progress is possible.

When the decoder gets stuck (which can happen with small K), an optional precode can add redundant packets before encoding, allowing recovery of more source packets. The decoder may also use inactivation decoding, treating some source packets as "inactive" and resuming belief propagation.
sections.plainLanguage: At each stop, mix the packets you have to make new ones. At the end, unmix them using math, recovering the original chunks piece by piece.

sections.title: Packet Format and Parameters
sections.content:
BATS embeds coding parameters into packets for intermediate nodes and the destination to know how to handle them. A 32-bit field encodes K (source packet count), M and q (batch size and field size), and BID (batch ID).

Each coded packet contains two parts: a coefficient vector (CO octets describing which source packets are mixed) and coded data (T octets). The total packet size (TO = T + CO) must fit within the network's Path MTU (maximum transmission unit).

The maximum K value is 2^16 - 1, and the maximum BID is 2^13 - 1 (8192 batches per session). This limits the maximum data deliverable in a single BATS session to approximately (PMTU - H - 10) * (2^16 - 1) octets, where H is the header length. For example, with PMTU = 1500, H = 50, and q = 2, M = 128, the maximum file size is roughly 20 MB.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet says: how many original chunks there were, how many I mixed in this batch, which batch, and the mixed data.

sections.title: Open Research Problems
sections.content:
The baseline BATS scheme described leaves several areas for refinement. Coding design: When K is small, the pseudorandom degree sampler may not protect all source packets evenly; deterministic degree sequences and better sampling for small K are needed. Adaptive recoding: Transmitting different numbers of recoded packets for different batches, based on batch rank, can improve efficiency. Batch interleaving: Bursty packet loss is reduced by transmitting packets from different batches in mixed order rather than batch-by-batch.

Multicast: While the baseline focuses on single-source, single-destination, BATS can support multiple sources and destinations, but requires statistically independent batches from different sources and different treatment of the inner code for multiple destinations.

Protocol design: Congestion control cannot be purely end-to-end because intermediate nodes control how many recoded packets they generate. Routing must account for the fact that flow rates are measured not by raw packet count (due to recoding), and packet counts are not conserved (different links may have different rates). Media access control can exploit the fact that retransmission is unnecessary and high loss rates are tolerated.

Security: BATS inherits eavesdropping resistance from fountain codes (when degree > batch size, recovering source packets requires 2^(-T) probability of guessing) and is vulnerable to pollution attacks if compromised nodes inject forged packets, which can spread through recoding and decoding. Homomorphic signatures and trusted computing are proposed countermeasures.
sections.plainLanguage: Refinements needed: getting the mix distribution right for small data, sending different amounts per batch, mixing up order to handle bursts, supporting multiple senders and receivers, rethinking network management, and defending against attackers and corrupted packets.
